headline: Paper Comes Back, the Grid Falls Behind and Seals Take the Blame
teaser: Were screens really to blame for falling test scores? Who should pay for AI's huge electricity bill? And would killing seals actually save salmon?

articles.title: Back to Pen and Paper: Norway Rethinks Screens in the Classroom
articles.dek: Norway was one of the world's keenest adopters of classroom tablets; now it is bringing printed textbooks back. Were screens the real problem, or the way they were used?
paras: Three years ago, a third-grade teacher in Norway named Pål Ludvig Finstad put his pupils' tablets away and handed out pencils and paper instead. Several of his pupils were struggling to read and write, and he believed they urgently needed a different approach. His school administration disagreed and gave him a written warning. Today, his decision looks less like rebellion and more like a preview of national policy. Norway, once one of the most enthusiastic adopters of classroom technology in the world, is now bringing printed textbooks back into its schools.

For nearly two decades, Norwegian education authorities encouraged schools to replace books with computers and tablets. The trend accelerated during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lessons moved online almost overnight, and from 2023 primary schools in Oslo were expected to provide a digital device for every single pupil. The reasoning seemed sound: children would grow up in a digital world, so school should prepare them for it. Devices also promised lighter school bags, instant access to information and lessons that could adapt to each learner.

The results, however, have been disappointing. In the 2025 round of PISA, the international test that compares 15-year-olds across dozens of countries, Norwegian students scored below the average of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in reading, mathematics and science. According to news reports, it was the first time since 2006 that the country had fallen below the average in all three areas at once. Researchers cannot say for certain what caused the decline, but distraction from screens is widely regarded as one plausible explanation. A Norwegian commission on screen use had already concluded in 2024 that students generally understand long texts better when they read them on paper.

The government's response has been swift. Officials plan to enshrine pupils' right to printed textbooks in law, and the city of Oslo has dropped its rule of one device per primary pupil, giving individual schools more freedom to decide. Authorities also recommend restricting mobile phones in schools and introducing artificial intelligence into the curriculum only gradually. Torgeir Micaelsen, the minister responsible for digitalisation, admitted that screens may have entered schools "too quickly," before anyone fully understood their effects or knew what good teaching with digital devices actually looked like.

Supporters of the change argue that the case for paper is about more than nostalgia. Reading a long printed text, they say, encourages the sustained attention that deep comprehension requires, whereas a tablet invites constant switching between apps, notifications and links. Handwriting may also help young children remember letters and words. From this perspective, Norway did not simply buy too many gadgets; it introduced a powerful tool without evidence that it improved learning, and children paid the price.

Not everyone accepts this explanation. Silje Ween, the head of a primary school, told the news agency AFP that "the screen itself is not the problem"; difficulties arise, she argued, when the tool becomes more important than the content. In her view, a book and a tablet can both be useful, and choosing one does not have to exclude the other. Critics of a full retreat also point out that pupils still need digital skills, such as judging whether online information is reliable, and that these skills will not develop if technology is simply removed from classrooms.

Others think the reforms do not go far enough. Christer Hyggen, a sociologist at OsloMet University, has described the measures as superficial. He argues that the deeper problems lie in how digital platforms are designed: addictive features, targeted advertising and the profiling of children's data. Norway is preparing a bill that would ban "harmful" platforms such as TikTok and Snapchat for children under 16, and it wants to temporarily ban camera-equipped smart glasses in places like schools and parks. Yet Hyggen believes that real change can only happen at a larger scale, across Europe as a whole, because a single small country has limited power over global technology companies.

Norway's experience offers a lesson for every country that has rushed to digitise education. Technology is neither a cure nor a poison; its value depends on how, when and why it is used. The challenge for Norwegian schools now is to avoid swinging from one extreme to the other—replacing an uncritical faith in screens with an equally uncritical faith in paper. Whether printed textbooks will raise test scores remains uncertain, but the debate has already forced educators to ask a question they skipped twenty years ago: what does the evidence actually say?

write.p:
Dr. Larsen: Norway is bringing printed textbooks back into schools after its students' test scores fell, and some say screens were introduced too quickly. Should schools limit the use of tablets and laptops in class? Why or why not?
Mia: "Yes. Screens are full of distractions, and research suggests we understand long texts better on paper. Schools should use devices only for specific tasks."
Kevin: "I disagree. The problem is not the device but how teachers use it. Students need digital skills for university and work, so removing screens would leave them unprepared."

articles.title: Faster Than the Grid: Who Should Pay for AI's Appetite for Power?
articles.dek: Data centres' demand for electricity is growing almost ten times faster than the US power grid. Should tech companies pay the full cost, or should everyone share it?
paras: Every time someone asks a chatbot a question or streams a video, a computer somewhere in a data centre does the work, and that computer needs electricity. As companies race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence, the demand for that electricity is growing at a remarkable speed. According to an analysis by the insurance broker Howden, the power used by data centres in the United States has risen by an average of 19% a year since 2000, while the country's grid capacity has expanded by only about 2% a year. In other words, demand has been growing nearly ten times faster than the system built to supply it.

The scale of investment is enormous. The bank Citigroup projects that large technology companies will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029. Data centres took about 5% of US grid capacity in 2025, and researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate that they could consume as much as 12% of the nation's electricity by 2028, roughly six times their 1.9% share in 2018.

Why can't the grid simply keep up? Rob Gramlich, president of the consulting firm Grid Strategies, describes the problem as a "mismatch in timing." A data centre can be built in a year or two, but new power lines and power plants require careful study and planning that can take many years. After roughly 25 years in which electricity demand barely grew, Gramlich says, utilities got out of practice at building new infrastructure. As a result, Kathryn Burke of the insurance firm Marsh expects around 50% to 60% of data centre projects to be delayed beyond the timelines their developers are counting on.

The bottleneck is not only a technical issue; it is also a question of fairness. A study by Cornell University researchers, published in the journal Nature Energy, found that data centres pushed up wholesale electricity prices in some regions in 2025, by nearly 20% in the southern San Francisco Bay Area and by about 17% around Dallas–Fort Worth. Across the four grids the researchers examined, data centres paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth: $3.12 billion out of an $8.25 billion bill. The rest fell on other customers, including ordinary households, for whom wholesale prices make up roughly 30% to 50% of a monthly bill.

Voters have noticed. In local ballot measures held on 3 November, residents rejected data centre development in 40 out of 41 cases. A survey by the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg Public Policy Center found that 61% of American adults, and 70% of those under 30, oppose new data centres in their area. Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organiser with the youth group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune that he was not excited about growing up having to compete with tech companies over water and energy prices. Some places have gone further: Ohio already has 125 local moratoriums on new data centres.

Defenders of the industry offer a different perspective. They argue that data centres bring investment, construction jobs and tax revenue, and that leadership in artificial intelligence matters for a country's economic future and security. In their view, the solution is not to block data centres but to make them supply more of their own power. Delaware became the first state to require large energy users to produce or secure all of their electricity, including a share of clean energy, within ten years of starting operations. A bill recently passed by the US Senate would also require data centres to pay for their energy use rather than drive up costs for neighbouring communities.

Yet "bring your own power" has drawbacks too. Many companies are turning to natural gas: the research firm BloombergNEF has tracked 181 gigawatts of gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centres, more than 90% of it in the United States. A Bloomberg News analysis suggests that the planned gas plants could raise emissions from the US power sector by 20%. Experts also warn that large, sudden swings in a data centre's demand can cause outages and damage on-site equipment, so private power plants are not a simple cure.

The debate ultimately turns on a basic question: who should bear the costs of a new technology whose benefits are spread unevenly? If data centres pay the full price of their electricity, AI may become more expensive and some projects may move elsewhere. If they do not, families who may never use advanced AI tools could end up subsidising them through their power bills. A fair compromise would probably require companies to cover the costs they create while governments speed up the planning of cleaner grids, but finding that balance will be one of the defining economic challenges of the AI era.

articles.title: Would Culling Seals Save Salmon? A Food-Web Model Says Probably Not
articles.dek: Seals and sea lions eat salmon, so killing them seems an obvious way to help the fish. A new study in Science suggests nature is not that simple.
paras: Along the Pacific coast of North America, salmon are much more than a food. They are central to Indigenous cultures, commercial fishing and the health of rivers and forests. Yet many populations of Chinook and coho salmon have declined so sharply that they are now listed as threatened or endangered. As the fish have struggled, another group of animals has thrived: seals and sea lions, whose numbers recovered after the United States banned most hunting of marine mammals in 1972. To many fishers and some lawmakers, the conclusion seems obvious: if seals eat salmon, killing seals should bring salmon back.

A study published in the journal Science on 19 November 2026 suggests the answer is far less simple. A team led by Dylan Gomes, of Oregon State University's Marine Mammal Institute and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), built a computer model of the ocean ecosystem off Northern California, Oregon and Washington. Instead of looking only at how many salmon seals eat, the model tracked who eats whom across the whole food web. The researchers then tested what would happen to Chinook and coho salmon if seals, sea lions, seabirds and other predators were reduced on a large scale.

Their conclusion was that widespread culling would do little to restore salmon populations. The reason lies in indirect effects. Seals and sea lions do eat salmon, but they also eat other fish, including Pacific hake, a far more abundant species that competes with young salmon for food and sometimes eats them. Remove the predators, and hake can multiply, which may cancel out any benefit to salmon. As the authors put it, broad culls "may do more harm than good." In the model, the strongest increase in salmon came not from killing seals but from reducing hake.

That does not mean fishing more hake is an easy answer. The researchers warn that a larger hake harvest could accidentally catch more salmon as bycatch and trigger other changes in the ecosystem. They also note that large-scale removals of marine mammals and seabirds would be expensive, difficult to carry out, and both ethically and socially problematic. Meanwhile, the ocean itself is changing: warming waters put major pressure on salmon, alongside dams, habitat loss and fishing, problems that no cull can solve.

Supporters of predator control see the issue differently. Wildlife managers point out that seals and sea lions often gather at narrow "bottlenecks," such as dams, bridges and fish ladders, where young or returning fish are easy to catch. Near Washington's Hood Canal Bridge, for example, studies have found that seals and sea lions can eat up to half of the young steelhead, a close relative of salmon, migrating past. A Washington state wildlife official, Nate Pamplin, told lawmakers in July that targeted removals of sea lions on the Columbia River since 2020 had saved an estimated 64,000 returning Chinook. Some tribal leaders, whose treaty rights protect their fisheries, add that certain animals have learned to ignore non-lethal deterrents.

Interestingly, the new study does not completely reject this view. It suggests that removing individual animals at specific bottlenecks may sometimes help, even though broad culls along the coast are likely to be costly and ineffective. This distinction matters for current politics. A bill introduced in the US Congress by two Washington representatives, one Republican and one Democrat, would expand the ability of federal, state and tribal authorities to remove seals and sea lions from Washington waters. Its supporters describe it as a tool to be used alongside habitat restoration rather than a complete solution.

Conservationists, however, worry that the predators are being blamed for a crisis with deeper roots. Casey Mclean, who runs a marine mammal rescue centre in Washington, notes that the salmon crisis has been going on for a very long time and that seals eat dozens of different fish species. A 2022 review commissioned by the Washington State Academy of Sciences reached a similar conclusion: while seals and sea lions can reduce salmon numbers in particular places, they are probably not a primary cause of the failure of salmon to recover.

The debate illustrates a common trap in environmental policy: focusing on the most visible culprit rather than the whole system. Killing a predator is a dramatic, easily understood action, while restoring rivers, removing dams or adapting to warmer oceans is slow and expensive. The Science study is a model, not a field experiment, and its results depend on the data fed into it. Still, it offers a valuable reminder that in nature every action has side effects, and that the most obvious solution is not always the most effective one.

write.p:
Dr. Nguyen: A new study suggests that killing large numbers of seals and sea lions would do little to bring back endangered salmon, because the predators also eat other fish that compete with salmon. Yet some managers say removing a few animals at dams and bridges does help. Should governments allow the killing of protected animals to save an endangered species? Why or why not?
